kurals.tamil:
வைத்தான்வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள் அஃதுண்ணான்
செத்தான் செயக்கிடந்தது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaiththaanvaai Saandra Perumporul Aqdhunnaan
Seththaan Seyakkitandhadhu Il
kurals.meaning: A man who fills his house with vast wealth and never enjoys it is as good as dead, for there is nothing that wealth has done through him.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a boy who fills his whole room with sweets but never eats one and never shares one. The sweets just sit there until they go stale. Valluvar says a person who piles up money like that and never uses it might as well not be there at all.
kurals.university: The chapter title நன்றியில் செல்வம் uses நன்றி in its older sense of 'benefit, good' rather than 'gratitude': this is wealth that does no good to anyone. In vaittaan-vaay (வைத்தான்வாய்) வாய் means 'place', so the wealth 'fills the place where he stored it'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses இடமெல்லாம் நிறைந்த, and Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) adds that the man does not eat it 'through avarice' (உலோபத்தால்). The second line is elliptical: seththaan (செத்தான்) can be read either as 'he is (equivalent to) a dead man', as Solomon Pappaiah and Pope take it ('Is dead'), or as 'when he dies, there is nothing left done (by the wealth)', as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it; both readings yield the same verdict that unused wealth achieves nothing. The chapter stands in the Kudiyiyal after Panbudaimai (ch. 100), turning from courtesy to the social uselessness of hoarded riches, and complements the earlier chapters on Ithal (ch. 23) and Oppuravu (ch. 22). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yajnavalkya prepares to divide his property and leave home, his wife Maitreyi asks whether the whole earth full of wealth would make her immortal; he answers that her life would merely be like that of the rich, for there is no hope of immortality through wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that riches, however vast, cannot purchase what matters most and are left behind at death.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it exposes wealth as powerless at the moment of death, so a life spent only storing it accomplishes nothing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; shares the futility-of-wealth-at-death theme but is about spiritual immortality rather than miserly non-use.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a rich man whose land yielded so much that he planned bigger barns to store it all and then take his ease; God calls him a fool, for that very night his soul is required of him, and the question is who will own what he has stored.
christianity.explanation: The parable condemns laying up treasure for oneself without being rich toward God or others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's hoarder, the rich fool dies beside his full storehouses having done nothing with them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a very close parallel of stored-up wealth left unused at sudden death.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an urges believers to spend from what God has provided before death comes, when a person will plead to be granted a short delay so that he could give charity and be among the righteous.
islam.explanation: Death ends the chance to make wealth do good, and the hoarder's regret comes too late.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of a man who dies with his wealth untouched and nothing accomplished.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong thematic match on wealth unused before death, though framed as charity rather than personal enjoyment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Every person will have to justify himself for everything his eye saw and which he did not eat.”
judaism.explanation: Rav teaches that refusing the lawful good things of life is itself something one must answer for; the Talmud adds that Rabbi Eleazar saved coins so he could taste every kind of food once a year.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise counts it a failure to own abundance and never enjoy it.
judaism.source: Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin 4:12 (tr. Heinrich W. Guggenheimer, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; matches the 'did not enjoy' half of the Kural, though its target is ascetic refusal rather than miserliness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just now, lord, a money-lending householder died in Savatthi. I have come from conveying his heirless fortune to the royal palace: eight million in silver, to say nothing of the gold. But even though he was a money-lending householder, his enjoyment of food was like this: he ate broken rice & pickle brine.”
buddhism.explanation: King Pasenadi reports a rich miser who lived like a pauper and died, his fortune passing to the crown; the Buddha says such wealth, not properly used, goes to waste.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's hoarder exactly: immense riches, none enjoyed, and nothing achieved by them at death.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one narrative illustration of the couplet.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who employs not his time in enjoying his property, or gives not of it to ascetics, but lays it up (like a miser)--at him, the foolish one, about to perish, his hoarded wealth shall mock, and the favour of the world shall mock.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain pictures the hoarder's own treasure mocking him as death approaches.
jainism.tie_back: It makes the same point as the Kural: wealth neither enjoyed nor given leaves its dying owner with nothing.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture, chosen because it is an almost exact parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas is granted his wish that whatever he touches turn to gold, and finds that his bread and wine also turn to gold, so that the richest man alive faces starvation amid his treasure until he begs the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that wealth which cannot be used for life's ordinary goods is worthless, even deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's miser, Midas is surrounded by riches that do nothing for him and bring him close to death.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; vivid parallel of unusable wealth, but Midas's problem is a curse, not miserly choice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Misers, he said, took care of property as if it belonged to them, but derived no more benefit from it than if it belonged to others.”
philosophy.explanation: The Cynic Bion of Borysthenes mocks misers as mere caretakers of goods they never actually use.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the hoarder gets nothing from the wealth he guards, as if he were already dead to it.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 4.50 (Bion), tr. R. D. Hicks (Wikisource)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource; strong match on owning without benefit.

kurals.tamil:
பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulaanaam Ellaamendru Eeyaadhu Ivarum
Marulaanaam Maanaap Pirappu
kurals.meaning: Thinking that wealth can do everything, a man clings to it and gives nothing away; that very delusion leads him to a debased birth.
kurals.elementary: Some people think, 'If I just have enough money, I'll have everything!' So they grip their money tight and never share. Valluvar says this is a big mistake, like a confused traveller holding the wrong map, and it leads them to a very sad place.
kurals.university: The first line reports the miser's creed, poruLaal aam ellaam ('by wealth everything is achieved'), and his conduct, eeyaadhu ivaRum ('not giving, he clings'); ivaRu- denotes tight-fisted holding, the same root as இவறல் (miserliness) condemned among royal faults in Kural 432. The second line names the result: maruL (மருள், 'delusion, bewilderment') produces maaNaap piRappu, 'an un-excellent birth'. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps this general ('a birth without distinction'), Kalaignar reads it this-worldly ('a base creature'), while Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation ('will be born a demon') follow the classical line that specifies a ghost or demon birth (பேய்ப் பிறப்பு); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as an endless, graceless cycle of births. The phrase மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு also closes Kural 351, where delusion about what is real is said to cause such a birth, so Valluvar here treats the miser's faith in money as a species of metaphysical error. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna describes the demoniac mentality that says, so much wealth is mine today and more will come tomorrow; deluded by such thoughts and bound by attachment, these persons fall into a foul hell and take birth again and again in demoniac wombs.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita traces degraded rebirth to the delusion of treating possessions as the measure of life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the delusion that wealth is everything produces a debased, even demonic, birth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; closely matches both the 'wealth is mine' delusion and the consequence of degraded birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a rich man who feasted every day while the beggar Lazarus lay starving at his gate; after death Lazarus is comforted while the rich man is in torment, reminded that he received his good things in his lifetime.
christianity.explanation: The parable shows a lifetime of withholding from the needy leading to a terrible state after death.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links refusal to give with a fallen condition in the life to come.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on withholding leading to a bad afterlife, though the 'wealth is everything' delusion is implicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to every scorner and mocker / Who collects wealth and [continuously] counts it. / He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal. / No! He will surely be thrown into the Crusher.”
islam.explanation: The surah condemns the man who hoards and counts his money, imagining it makes him invulnerable.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's deluded miser who believes wealth is everything and so earns a degraded destiny.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; near one-to-one on the false faith in wealth and its dire consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists among human characters the one who says, what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours, calls it an ordinary type, and records that some call it the character of Sodom.
judaism.explanation: Refusing ever to share, even when it costs nothing, is identified with the proverbially wicked city.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's miser who gives nothing displays exactly this Sodom-like closed-handedness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the refusal to give, but lacks the Kural's point about delusion and rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Petavatthu, a canonical collection of ghost stories, repeatedly explains that beings were reborn as hungry ghosts (petas) because in their human lives they were stingy and refused to give, even to ascetics who came for alms.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching makes miserliness (macchariya) a direct cause of rebirth in the ghost realm.
buddhism.tie_back: It closely matches the classical reading of the Kural that the miser's delusion leads to a ghost-like birth.
buddhism.source: Petavatthu (Khuddaka Nikaya), stories of misers reborn as petas
buddhism._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of a recurring Petavatthu theme rather than a single verified story; strong doctrinal match to the ghost-birth reading.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you.”
jainism.explanation: Queen Kamalâvatî rebukes King Ishukâra for wanting to seize a renouncer's abandoned property, teaching that no amount of wealth can satisfy or protect the soul.
jainism.tie_back: It directly contradicts the miser's creed in the Kural that wealth can accomplish everything.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; refutes the 'wealth is everything' delusion, though it does not mention degraded rebirth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Croesus of Lydia shows Solon his treasuries and asks who is the happiest of men, expecting to be named; Solon instead names obscure Athenians who lived and died well, and warns that no one should be called happy until his end is seen.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus's confidence that riches equal happiness is exposed as an illusion, later borne out by his fall.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus embodies the Kural's mistaken belief that wealth is everything.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good match on the delusion, but Croesus is not a miser and there is no rebirth element.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But meanness is both incurable (for old age and every disability is thought to make men mean) and more innate in men than prodigality; for most men are fonder of getting money than of giving.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle judges stinginess a deeper and harder vice to cure than wastefulness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats tight-fisted clinging to wealth as a deep-rooted error with grave consequences.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; fits the vice of withholding but not the specific delusion or its karmic result.

kurals.tamil:
ஈட்டம் இவறி இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர்
தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Eettam Ivari Isaiventaa Aatavar
Thotram Nilakkup Porai
kurals.meaning: Men who are greedy only for piling up wealth and care nothing for an honourable name are, by their very existence, a burden to the earth.
kurals.elementary: Think of a squirrel that hides a thousand nuts and never lets another animal have one, and no one in the forest has a kind word for it. Valluvar says people who only collect and collect, and never do anything good that others would remember, are just heavy weight on the ground.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two objects of desire against each other: eettam (ஈட்டம், 'accumulation', from ஈட்டு- 'to earn, amass') and isai (இசை, 'fame, renown'), which in the Kural is earned chiefly by giving (compare Pugazh, ch. 24, beginning 'ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல்'). Those who 'cling to accumulation and do not want renown' have a thoatram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, birth, existence') that is poRai (பொறை, 'burden, weight') to the earth; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read தோற்றம் as 'being born and living', Pope as appearing 'on the stage of being'. Solomon Pappaiah adds a competitive nuance: they want to amass more than others. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இசை as 'interest/inclination' (இசைவு) beyond acquiring wealth, a minority interpretation. The 'burden of the earth' image echoes Kural 239, where the land bearing a body without fame loses its yield. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that one who does not take part in the cycle of sacrifice and sharing set in motion for the world, but lives only for the satisfaction of the senses, lives in vain.
hinduism.explanation: A life that only takes and never contributes back to the common order is declared futile.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it judges the purely acquisitive life a dead weight on the world.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good match on a useless self-centred life, but sacrifice rather than fame is the missing element.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of a fig tree that bore no fruit for three years; the owner orders it cut down, asking why it should take up the ground, and the gardener pleads for one more year.
christianity.explanation: A barren life that produces nothing for others merely occupies space.
christianity.tie_back: The parable's tree that only 'cumbers the ground' is the Kural's man who is a burden to the earth.
christianity.source: Luke 13:6–9 (Parable of the Barren Fig Tree)
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; striking match on the 'burden to the ground' image, though the parable concerns repentance rather than wealth and fame.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an warns that rivalry in piling up worldly increase distracts people until they reach their graves, when they will surely come to know its emptiness.
islam.explanation: Competitive accumulation is portrayed as a diversion that fills a whole life and leaves nothing worthwhile.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's men obsessed with accumulation and indifferent to true honour.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the futility of accumulation, without the Kural's 'burden to the earth' image.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Shimon teaches that there are three crowns, of Torah, of priesthood and of royalty, but the crown of a good name surpasses them all.
judaism.explanation: A good name earned by one's deeds is ranked above every inherited dignity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural condemns those who prize hoarding over exactly this good name.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; affirms the value of a good name but does not address the burden of the acquisitive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that misers do not go to heavenly realms and fools do not praise generosity, but the wise person rejoices in giving and is happy hereafter.
buddhism.explanation: The verse sets the stingy fool against the generous wise person whose giving brings joy and good standing.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarders who care nothing for renown are the Dhammapada's misers who scorn generosity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best match on miser versus giver, lacking the specific contrast of hoarding with fame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who have, to the best of their ability, practised to any extent trifling acts of charity, will in another birth become great; while those who, when they have become wealthy, say, We will give alms some time or other, shall be punished and shall perish from all the sea-surrounded earth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet contrasts small, real generosity with the wealthy man's endless postponement of giving.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees the wealthy non-giver as having no rightful place on the earth.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text; good match on the wealthy non-giver and the earth, but renown is not its focus.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A fragment of the epic Cypria tells that Zeus, seeing the broad-bosomed Earth weighed down by the countless tribes of men, took pity on her and resolved to lighten her burden through the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth imagines humanity itself as a weight the Earth can groan under.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of people whose existence is a burden to the earth, though not its moral about hoarding.
greek_mythology.source: Cypria, fragment 1 (preserved in the scholia to Iliad 1.5)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best only: the 'burden on the earth' image matches, but the myth concerns population, not greed or fame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that liberality and beneficence win people's goodwill and lasting glory, while wealth hoarded or spent only on oneself earns none.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, true and lasting renown is gained by using one's means to help others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural blames exactly those who pursue accumulation and neglect the renown that giving would bring.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Cicero's argument on liberality and glory; reasonable fit, not verified verbatim this session.

kurals.tamil:
எச்சமென்று என்எண்ணுங் கொல்லோ ஒருவரால்
நச்சப் படாஅ தவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Echchamendru Enennung Kollo Oruvaraal
Nachchap Pataaa Thavan
kurals.meaning: What can a man whom no one loves expect to leave behind him as his legacy?
kurals.elementary: When a kind teacher retires, the children remember her stories and her hugs for years. But if someone never helped anyone, what will people remember about him when he is gone? Valluvar asks: what is left of a person nobody loved?
kurals.university: The key word is echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder, what is left over'), which in the Kural can mean posterity or a lasting name; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss 'what remains after his death', Solomon Pappaiah 'what will stand to recall him after his time'. The man is described as oruvaraal nachchap padaaa-thavan, 'one not desired by even a single person'; nachchu (நச்சு, 'to desire, love') returns in Kural 1008, where the same unloved man's wealth is a poisonous tree, so the chapter plays on நச்சு 'love' and நச்சு 'poison'. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason for his unpopularity, that he helped no one. Pope's explanation narrows echcham to what the miser can count as his own 'in the world to come', a reading that follows the classical tendency to interpret legacy in terms of merit for the next life. The rhetorical question (என் எண்ணும் கொல்லோ, 'what, pray, does he think?') turns the couplet into a mock of the miser's planning. The text is identical on both sources (ytamizh prints எண்ணுங் with the same ங்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that in the next world neither father nor mother, wife, sons nor kin remain as one's companions; leaving the body on the ground like a log, relatives turn away, and spiritual merit alone follows the dead.
hinduism.explanation: Only the good one has done survives a person; everything else is left behind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved hoarder has done no good, so nothing worthwhile remains of him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on 'what remains' after death, but does not address being unloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells his hearers not to lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust corrupt and thieves steal, but to lay up treasures in heaven, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
christianity.explanation: Earthly hoards vanish; only what is invested in goodness endures.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question of the miser: what lasting treasure has he laid up?
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on lasting legacy versus perishable wealth, but lacks the Kural's focus on being loved by no one.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an says that wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for one's hope.
islam.explanation: Possessions are passing ornaments; only lasting good deeds (al-baqiyat al-salihat, 'the things that remain') endure.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's miser, having done no good, has none of these 'remaining' deeds to leave behind.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the 'things that remain' phrase closely parallels echcham, though love from others is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that when a person departs, neither silver nor gold nor precious stones and pearls accompany him, but only Torah and good deeds.
judaism.explanation: Wealth stays behind at death; only learning and good deeds go with a person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks what the hoarder who has earned no one's love can possibly leave or take with him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on what endures beyond death; love from others is implicit only.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says the fool frets, thinking, I have sons, I have wealth, yet he is not even his own master, so how can sons or wealth be his?
buddhism.explanation: Possessions and family give no lasting hold to someone who does not even possess himself.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved miser likewise has nothing that will truly remain as his.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best match on the emptiness of possessions, without the theme of being unloved.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
jainism.explanation: The queen tells King Ishukâra that at death only dharma remains as a refuge, not property.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what the man who has won no one's love by giving can hope to have left; the Jain answer is only the Law he practised.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on what remains after death, while the theme of being unloved is not present.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, refusing Agamemnon's lavish gifts, says that cattle and treasure can be won by raiding but a man's life cannot be recovered, and that his mother foretold a choice between a long, obscure life and an early death with imperishable glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: In heroic thought, what outlasts a person is kleos, the remembered name, not possessions.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's unloved miser has no such remembered name to leave behind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best only: shares the idea of a lasting name over wealth, but in a warrior context unrelated to miserliness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The aged Cephalus tells Socrates that the greatest benefit of wealth for a decent man is that, as death approaches, he need not depart owing sacrifices to the gods or money to anyone, having cheated no one.
philosophy.explanation: For Cephalus, wealth matters at the end only for the clean account it lets a man leave behind.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural presses the same end-of-life question on the miser: what will he have left that counts?
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best: shares the theme of what wealth leaves at death, but does not address being unloved.

kurals.tamil:
கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்க்கு அடுக்கிய
கோடியுண் டாயினும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kotuppadhooum Thuyppadhooum Illaarkku Atukkiya
Kotiyun Taayinum Il
kurals.meaning: For those who neither give nor enjoy, wealth amounts to nothing, even if they possess crores heaped upon crores.
kurals.elementary: If you have a big box of crayons but never draw with them and never lend them to a friend, it is just like having no crayons at all. Valluvar says money works the same way: if you never use it and never share it, you are really poor.
kurals.university: The couplet names the two proper uses of wealth, koduppadhu (கொடுப்பது, 'giving') and thuyppadhu (துய்ப்பது, 'enjoying, consuming'), with the emphatic lengthening -ūum (கொடுப்பதூஉம், துய்ப்பதூஉம்) marking each as indispensable. Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) means 'crores stacked one upon another'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'many crores ever increasing'. The verdict il (இல், 'there is not') says such people are effectively without wealth; Pope renders the sense as 'they are poor'. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualifier that giving should be to those in need and enjoying should be as need requires, guarding against reading the couplet as licence for extravagance. The two-fold scheme parallels the Sanskrit gnomic triad of dāna, bhoga and nāśa (giving, enjoyment, destruction) found in Bhartrihari. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrihari's well-known stanza says that wealth has only three possible courses, giving, enjoyment and destruction; for the man who neither gives nor enjoys, the third course is what becomes of it.
hinduism.explanation: Wealth not given or used is bound simply to be lost.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own scheme of giving and enjoying, with the same conclusion that otherwise the wealth amounts to nothing.
hinduism.source: Bhartrihari, Nītiśataka (dānaṃ bhogo nāśas tisro gatayo bhavanti vittasya; verse numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from a well-attested stanza, not verified against a live translation this session; near one-to-one conceptual match.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich not to trust in uncertain riches but in God, who gives us richly all things to enjoy, and to be rich in good works, ready to distribute and willing to share.
christianity.explanation: Wealth is meant both to be enjoyed with gratitude and to be shared generously.
christianity.tie_back: It names the same two uses, enjoying and giving, that the Kural says give wealth its meaning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close structural match on enjoyment plus sharing.

islam.quote_or_event: “A servant says, My wealth. my wealth, but out of his wealth three things are only his: whatever he eats and makes use of or by means of which he dresses himself and it wears out or he gives as charity, and this is what he stored for himself (as a reward for the Hereafter), and what is beyond this (it is of no use to you) because you are to depart and leave it for other people.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that only what one consumes or gives away is truly one's own; the rest is merely left behind.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's teaching: wealth neither used nor given is as good as nothing to its owner.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a near one-to-one match on enjoying and giving as wealth's only real uses.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs observes that one person gives freely and yet grows richer, while another withholds more than is right and only comes to want.
judaism.explanation: Withholding does not make one rich; generosity does.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the one who never gives is poor despite heaped-up crores.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the paradox of the withholder's poverty, though it omits enjoyment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that rightly earned wealth should be used to bring pleasure to oneself, to parents, family and workers, to friends, to protect against losses, and to make offerings to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, devas and contemplatives.
buddhism.explanation: Wealth's benefits lie in using it for one's own and others' good, not in storing it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's pairing of enjoyment and giving as the purpose of riches.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on wealth's proper uses, distinct from the Hindu and Jain entries.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who, though utterly poor, will not beg, are the truly rich. Even the rich are poor if they give not.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrain redefines riches by conduct: the non-giver is poor whatever he owns.
jainism.tie_back: It restates the Kural's verdict that crores amount to nothing for one who does not give.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text, near one-to-one on giving, though it does not mention enjoyment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable a miser buries his gold and visits it daily; when a thief steals it and he laments, a neighbour advises him to bury a stone in its place, since it will serve him just as well as the gold he never used.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wealth that is never used has no more value than a stone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that unused, ungiven crores amount to nothing.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, 'The Miser and His Gold'
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a Greek fable (not myth proper); near one-to-one in moral.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle remarks that being rich consists in using things rather than in owning them, since it is the actual use of possessions that constitutes wealth.
philosophy.explanation: Wealth is defined by its use, not by mere ownership.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise denies that unused, ungiven riches are wealth at all.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close conceptual match, not verified verbatim this session.

kurals.tamil:
ஏதம் பெருஞ்செல்வம் தான்துவ்வான் தக்கார்க்கொன்று
ஈதல் இயல்பிலா தான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Edham Perunjelvam Thaandhuvvaan Thakkaarkkondru
Eedhal Iyalpilaa Thaan
kurals.meaning: One who neither enjoys his great wealth himself nor has it in his nature to give something to the worthy is a blight upon that wealth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a lovely garden where the owner never sits and never lets anyone else pick a flower. The garden is wasted, and the owner is like a sickness that keeps it from doing any good. Valluvar says a stingy rich person is like that sickness for his own money.
kurals.university: The opening word edham (ஏதம், 'harm, fault, affliction, disease') is the predicate, and its subject is the man described in the rest of the couplet: thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், 'he himself does not enjoy') and thakkaarkku ondru eedhal iyalbu ilaan (தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பு இலான், 'one who has no disposition to give even one thing to the worthy'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar therefore read him as a disease (நோய்) to his own great wealth, as does Pope's explanation ('a disease to his wealth'); Solomon Pappaiah inverts it, making the wealth a disease in his keeping, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads that he does harm to himself. The word iyalbu (இயல்பு, 'nature') stresses that the fault is temperamental, not circumstantial, and thakkaar (தக்கார், 'the deserving') narrows the duty of giving to worthy recipients, a classical criterion of proper gifts. Pope's verse rendering ('misery to men of churlish heart') follows the alternative sense. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that the righteous who eat what remains after offering are freed from sin, while those who prepare food only for their own enjoyment eat nothing but sin.
hinduism.explanation: Possessions kept wholly to oneself turn into a source of fault rather than blessing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees self-enclosed wealth as a blight rather than a good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on wealth becoming fault when not shared, though the Kural's miser does not even enjoy it himself.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Preacher calls it a grievous evil he has seen under the sun: riches kept by their owner to his own hurt, which are then lost in some misfortune so that nothing is left.
christianity.explanation: Hoarded riches can harm the very person who guards them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes the miser and his wealth a mutual affliction.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; very close on hoarded wealth as harm.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that withheld wealth becomes a burden and torment to the one who withholds it.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's claim that the non-giver's great wealth turns into an affliction.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on withheld wealth becoming harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah describes four kinds of givers, and calls wicked the one who neither wishes to give himself nor wants others to give.
judaism.explanation: Total unwillingness to give is classed as wickedness, not mere thrift.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's man with 'no nature for giving' fits this wicked type.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on the ungiving temperament, without the image of wealth as affliction.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that if beings knew, as he knows, the results of giving and sharing, they would not eat without having given, and the stain of selfishness would not overcome their minds.
buddhism.explanation: Stinginess is a mental stain; generosity, even of the last mouthful, is the remedy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man without a giving nature is overcome by exactly this stain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on the giving disposition, but lacks the 'disease to his wealth' image.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The seeking to accumulate wealth is a cause of vexation. The guarding that collected shining wealth causes vexation. Again, if any of that wealth which is so guarded be diminished, there is vexation. If it be lost, how great the vexation! Truly this said wealth is the very abode of vexation.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet shows hoarded wealth as nothing but a source of trouble at every stage.
jainism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's description of great wealth unenjoyed and ungiven as an affliction (ஏதம்).
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text; strong on hoarded wealth as affliction, though it reverses who afflicts whom.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus sees Tantalus standing in a pool beneath trees laden with fruit; whenever he stoops to drink the water vanishes, and whenever he reaches for the fruit the wind tosses it away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus suffers eternal want in the very midst of plenty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's miser, he is surrounded by goods that bring him only torment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best: the plenty-as-torment image fits, but Tantalus is punished by the gods, not by his own miserliness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Referring to a wealthy miser he said, He has not acquired a fortune; the fortune has acquired him.”
philosophy.explanation: Bion of Borysthenes jokes that the miser is possessed by his wealth rather than possessing it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise sees the non-enjoying, non-giving rich man as a bad relation to his own wealth.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 4.50 (Bion), tr. R. D. Hicks (Wikisource)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; captures the inverted owner–wealth relation, without the duty to give to the worthy.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான் செல்வம் மிகநலம்
பெற்றாள் தமியள்மூத் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Atraarkkondru Aatraadhaan Selvam Mikanalam
Petraal Thamiyalmooth Thatru
kurals.meaning: The wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a woman of great beauty who grows old alone, her gifts wasted.
kurals.elementary: Picture the most beautiful flower blooming inside a locked room where nobody ever sees it, until it slowly fades. Valluvar says money that never helps poor people is like that hidden flower: something lovely, wasted.
kurals.university: Atraar (அற்றார், 'those who have nothing, the destitute') are the intended recipients, and aatraadhaan (ஆற்றாதான்) is 'one who does not do (even one thing) for them'. The simile mika nalam petraaL thamiyaL mooththatru (மிக நலம் பெற்றாள் தமியள் மூத்தற்று) compares such wealth to 'a woman endowed with great beauty growing old alone'; Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation specify 'without a husband', Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep 'alone'. The point of the comparison is waste: a good thing that exists to be shared lapses unused, the same logic as the chapter's poisonous-tree image in 1008 and its counterpart in Kural 216, where a generous man's wealth is a fruit tree in the middle of the village. The simile reflects the social world of classical Tamil literature, in which beauty fulfilled in married life is the norm; modern readers may note the period assumption while keeping the moral about unshared resources. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man with food in store who, when the needy comes in miserable case begging for bread to eat, / Hardens his heart against him-even when of old he did him service-finds not one to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn on liberality condemns the man who refuses food to the needy and promises him a friendless end.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise condemns wealth that does nothing for the destitute.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on refusing the destitute, without the image of wasted beauty.

christianity.quote_or_event: John asks how the love of God can dwell in anyone who has this world's goods, sees a brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion against him.
christianity.explanation: Possessions withheld from the needy are a sign that love is absent.
christianity.tie_back: It condemns exactly the Kural's wealthy man who gives nothing to the destitute.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on refusing the needy, lacking the waste simile.

islam.quote_or_event: Surat al-Ma'un describes the one who denies the Judgement as he who drives away the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the poor, and condemns those who withhold even small kindnesses.
islam.explanation: Refusing basic help to the destitute is presented as a mark of spiritual bankruptcy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's man who does not give even one thing to the destitute is the Ma'un's withholder.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on withholding from the poor, but lacks the image of wasted beauty.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah commands that if there is a needy person among your brethren, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand, but open your hand wide and lend him enough for his need.
judaism.explanation: Withholding from the poor is forbidden; generosity to the needy is a commandment.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural blames the rich man who 'does not do one thing' for the destitute.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the duty to the destitute, without the simile of waste.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like water in a haunted place that, without being imbibed, dries up: such is the wealth acquired by a worthless person who neither enjoys it himself nor gives.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares unshared wealth to pure water in a place no one dares to drink from, which simply evaporates.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's beauty growing old alone, it pictures a good thing that withers unused because it is never shared.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta, closing verse (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the simile of a wasted, unused good closely mirrors the Kural's.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The great wealth which the miserly-minded have attained, who neither know how to give it away nor to use it themselves, shall be like the beauteous damsels of a family, who when they have arrived at puberty are enjoyed by others; i.e. others than its owner shall enjoy it.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet uses the same image of a young woman's beauty to show that a miser's wealth benefits others, never its owner.
jainism.tie_back: Both texts compare unshared wealth to feminine beauty that its keeper does not rightly bring to fruition.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text with a strikingly similar simile, though its point (others enjoy it) differs from the Kural's (beauty wasted).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The beautiful youth Narcissus, sought by many, scorns every suitor, and in the end falls in love with his own reflection and wastes away beside the pool, his beauty consumed without ever being shared.
greek_mythology.explanation: Beauty turned wholly inward withers without bringing joy to anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural's image of great beauty fading in solitude as a picture of wasted, unshared riches.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best: the wasted-beauty image matches, but the myth is about self-love, not wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now the things that have a use may be used either well or badly; and riches is a useful thing; and everything is used best by the man who has the virtue concerned with it; riches, therefore, will be used best by the man who has the virtue concerned with wealth; and this is the liberal man.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that wealth exists to be used, and is used best by the generous person.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's simile makes the same claim negatively: wealth not used for the needy wastes its purpose.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on wealth's purpose being use, without the Kural's focus on the destitute.

kurals.tamil:
நச்சப் படாதவன் செல்வம் நடுவூருள்
நச்சு மரம்பழுத் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Nachchap Pataadhavan Selvam Natuvoorul
Nachchu Marampazhuth Thatru
kurals.meaning: The wealth of a man whom nobody loves is like a poisonous tree bearing fruit in the middle of the town.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a tree in the middle of the playground covered in shiny fruit, but the fruit is poisonous, so nobody can eat it. Valluvar says a selfish rich person's money is like that tree: right there in front of everyone, but no use to anyone.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a pun: nachchap padaadhavan (நச்சப் படாதவன், 'one not loved', from நச்சு- 'to desire') and nachchu maram (நச்சு மரம், 'poison tree'). Pope's explanation identifies it as the etty tree (எட்டி, the nux-vomica, Strychnos nux-vomica), and Sivayogi Sivakumar quotes the proverb எட்டி பழுத்தால் என்ன, ஈயாதான் வாழ்ந்தால் என்ன ('what if the etty ripens, what if the non-giver prospers'). The setting naduvooruL (நடுவூருள், 'in the middle of the town') heightens the irony: the fruit is in full view and within reach of all, yet useless. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason the man is unloved, that he helps no one. The image is the exact inverse of Kural 216, where the wealth of the generous is a fruit-bearing tree in the midst of the village, so Valluvar deliberately pairs the two chapters on Oppuravu and Nandriyil Selvam. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No friend is he who to his friend and comrade who comes imploring food, will offer nothing. / Let him depart-no home is that to rest in-, and rather seek a stranger to support him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic poet says the one who offers nothing to those who come to him is no friend, and his house is no refuge.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is just such a 'house that is no home': present in the town but of no use to anyone.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.4 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on the useless, friendless rich man, without the tree image.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs says that the people curse the one who withholds grain, but blessing rests on the head of the one who sells it.
christianity.explanation: The hoarder of what others need earns the community's hatred.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's unloved man whose wealth benefits no one is the hoarder the people curse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on the community's resentment of useless hoarded wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi says the generous person is near to God, near to people and near to Paradise, while the miser is far from God, far from people and far from Paradise.
islam.explanation: Miserliness is pictured as distance from everyone, divine and human.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's miser whom no one loves and whose wealth no one can approach.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good thematic fit, but Tirmidhi himself grades this narration gharib and many scholars consider it weak (da'if).

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud says the people of Sodom grew arrogant through their abundance and resolved to stop travellers coming among them, since visitors would only diminish their wealth.
judaism.explanation: Sodom's riches, sealed off from strangers and the poor, became a byword for wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's poisonous tree in the town, Sodom's plenty stood in full view yet was deliberately made useless to others.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on wealth deliberately kept from others, though not focused on the individual's being unloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells General Siha that a giver, a master of giving, is dear and charming to people at large, and that good people associate with him.
buddhism.explanation: Generosity makes a person beloved; its absence leaves one unloved.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural describes the reverse case: the non-giver whom no one loves and whose wealth no one enjoys.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches by inversion, without the tree image.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The bat will not go to the rough-stemmed wood-apple tree, though near and fruitful. So the riches of those who, though they be very near to one, have no greatness of soul, have not the excellence of being considered as profitable.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet compares the riches of small-souled men to a fruitful tree near at hand that no creature will approach.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's own tree image: wealth close by and laden with fruit, yet of no benefit to anyone.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 27 ('Riches without goodness'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text with a very close tree simile.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes' comedy, Ploutos, the god of Wealth, is blind and so visits the wicked and the stingy instead of the good; when his sight is restored, he leaves the unworthy rich and enriches the deserving.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play mocks wealth that sits with the undeserving where it does no good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is precisely the undeserving holder of wealth that benefits no one.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best: wealth misplaced with the unworthy, but no direct parallel to the poison-tree image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius has Lady Philosophy argue that money shows its worth in being spent rather than hoarded, and that avarice makes men hated while generosity makes them famous.
philosophy.explanation: Hoarding not only wastes money but makes its owner odious.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's unloved rich man is hated for the same avarice that makes his wealth useless.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy II, prose 5
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; close on hated avarice and useless hoarding.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பொரீஇத் தற்செற்று அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய
ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anporeeith Tharsetru Aranokkaadhu Eettiya
Onporul Kolvaar Pirar
kurals.meaning: Shining wealth gathered by abandoning love, denying oneself, and ignoring righteousness will in the end be taken by others.
kurals.elementary: A boy saves all his pocket money, never shares, never buys himself a treat, and even cheats a little to get more. One day he moves away and leaves the jar behind, and other kids spend it. Valluvar says money gathered in such a selfish, unhappy way ends up with someone else.
kurals.university: The couplet lists three things sacrificed in the getting: anbu oreei (அன்பு ஒரீஇ, 'having forsaken love', the -īi lengthening marking the verbal participle), thaR setRu (தற்செற்று, 'having afflicted oneself', i.e. denying oneself comfort), and aRam nokkaadhu (அறம் நோக்காது, 'without regard for virtue'). The resulting oNporuL (ஒண்பொருள், 'bright, glittering wealth') is taken by piRar (பிறர், 'others'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Sivayogi Sivakumar read 'others will enjoy it', Kalaignar sharpens it to 'others will plunder it', and Pope's explanation has 'strangers will inherit'; Pope glosses the three omissions as friendship, comfort and charity. Pappaiah reads anbu as love shown to others through giving, which ties the couplet to the chapter's theme rather than to domestic affection. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this world is pervaded by the Lord; enjoy it through renunciation, and do not covet, for whose is wealth?
hinduism.explanation: Wealth never truly belongs to anyone, so grasping at it is futile.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder discovers this when the wealth he amassed passes to others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on the non-ownership of wealth, though the Upanishad's focus is spiritual renunciation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher portrays a solitary man who toils endlessly and denies himself, never asking who will benefit.
christianity.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural's three omissions, love, self-care and wisdom, and the question of who will finally have the wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; near one-to-one on loveless, self-depriving accumulation for unknown others.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who among you considers the wealth of his heirs dearer to him than his own wealth?” They replied, “O Allah's Messenger! There is none among us but loves his own wealth more.” The Prophet said, “So his wealth is whatever he spends (in Allah's Cause) during his life (on good deeds) while the wealth of his heirs is whatever he leaves after his death.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that what one does not spend on good belongs, in truth, to one's heirs.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that wealth amassed without virtue or generosity is really gathered for others.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; near one-to-one on unspent wealth belonging to others.

judaism.quote_or_event: When King Monobaz gave away his treasures in a famine, his relatives protested; he replied that his fathers had stored treasures below and for others, while he was storing them above and for himself.
judaism.explanation: Giving converts wealth into a treasure one truly keeps; hoarding merely saves it for others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that wealth hoarded without virtue goes to others.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on hoarded wealth being 'for others', from a distinctly rabbinic source.

buddhism.quote_or_event: A deva tells the Buddha that when a house is on fire, the vessel carried out is of use, not what burns inside; so, since the world is ablaze with aging and death, one should take out wealth by giving, for what is given is well saved.
buddhism.explanation: Only wealth given away is truly rescued; what is kept is lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hoarder, who never gave, loses all his amassed wealth to others.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on wealth lost unless given, though the 'others take it' element is implicit.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Leaving behind bipeds and quadrupeds, his fields, his house, his wealth, his corn, and everything; against his will, and accompanied only by his Karman, he enters a new existence, either a good or a bad one. When they have burned with fire on the funeral pile his forlorn, helpless corpse, his wife and sons and kinsfolk will choose another man to provide for them.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns King Brahmadatta that at death all property is left behind and others carry on, while only one's karma goes with the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that wealth gathered without regard for dharma passes to others, leaving its gatherer only the karma of how he got it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong canonical parallel on property left to others and karma alone accompanying the soul.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Cyrus's troops sack Sardis, the captured Croesus tells Cyrus that the soldiers are not plundering his city or his treasures, for nothing is his any longer, but are carrying off what now belongs to Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The richest king of his age sees his hoard pass in a single day to another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus's fate illustrates the Kural's warning that amassed wealth is finally taken by others.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on wealth passing to others, though Croesus's loss is by conquest, not loveless hoarding.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Horace reminds Postumus that the years slip away and death comes for all, and that a worthier heir will drink the Caecuban wine he guarded behind a hundred locks.
philosophy.explanation: What one jealously hoards will be enjoyed by an heir after one's death.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's verdict that the hoarder's shining wealth will be taken by others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Roman moral poetry rather than formal philosophy; very close on the heir enjoying the hoard.

kurals.tamil:
சீருடைச் செல்வர் சிறுதுனி மாரி
வறங்கூர்ந் தனையது உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Seerutaich Chelvar Sirudhuni Maari
Varangoorn Thanaiyadhu Utaiththu
kurals.meaning: The brief poverty of generous, honoured rich men is like a rain cloud that has emptied itself for a while; it will soon be full again.
kurals.elementary: A rain cloud pours out all its water on the thirsty fields, and for a little while it looks thin and empty. But soon it fills up again. Valluvar says when kind, generous people run short for a while, it is just like that cloud: they gave a lot, and they will be full again.
kurals.university: After nine couplets on useless wealth, the chapter closes on its positive counterpart. Seerudaich chelvar (சீருடைச் செல்வர்) are 'rich men endowed with excellence', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'famous' and Solomon Pappaiah 'famous for giving to others'. Their siRu thuni (சிறுதுனி) is 'a small distress', read by most commentators as a brief poverty; Pope renders 'brief poverty'. It is compared to maari vaRam koorndhanaiyadhu (மாரி வறங் கூர்ந்தனையது), 'like the rain cloud becoming impoverished', i.e. temporarily spent; Mu. Varadarasanar specifies 'the cloud that can protect the world'. The implication is that the generous man's want is temporary and itself a sign of his giving, as the cloud's emptiness follows its rain. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes a different line, reading the distress as the darkening that precedes rain and turns into good; Kalaignar reads the couplet as saying that even a shadow of poverty on such men is as grave as failed rain. The cloud image recalls Kural 211 on duty that expects no return, like the rain. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the rich satisfy the poor implorer, and bend his eye upon a longer pathway. / Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic poet urges the rich to give, knowing that fortune turns like a chariot wheel.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a giver's changes of fortune as passing turns of the wheel rather than lasting loss.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on giving and the transience of fortune, without the cloud image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth: and if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be.”
christianity.explanation: In a passage urging generous giving (casting bread on the waters, giving a portion to seven and eight), the Preacher points to clouds that pour out what they hold.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image: the generous rich empty themselves like rain clouds.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the cloud image and generous context match, though the verse does not say the cloud refills.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an assures believers that whatever they spend in charity, God will replace it, for He is the best of providers.
islam.explanation: Spending for good does not finally impoverish the giver; it is replenished.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that the generous man's want is temporary, like a spent cloud that will fill again.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on replenishment after giving, without the cloud image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person will never become impoverished from giving charity. No harm nor damage will ever be caused because of charity”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that charity never truly impoverishes the giver.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats the generous rich man's poverty as brief and not real ruin.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good fit, though Maimonides denies the poverty altogether while the Kural admits a brief one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In a verse spoken to the Buddha, devas say that those who share even from the little they have, like fellow travellers on the road, do not die among the dead.
buddhism.explanation: Generosity under scarcity is especially praised and never truly lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural honours the generous rich even in their short-lived poverty.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good on generosity amid scarcity, but no image of temporary depletion and renewal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though they live near the mighty ocean whose waters overflow, men look on the spring of a small well whose water is almost dried up and live. The poverty of the great is better than the riches of those who know not of the next birth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain poet says people still draw life from a nearly dry spring rather than the vast salt sea, and so the noble in poverty are worth more than the rich who give nothing.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's spent rain cloud, the noble man's depleted state is still a source of life for others.
jainism.source: Nāladiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a Tamil Jain text with a close water image for the generous man's poverty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon generously share their meagre food with disguised gods whom richer households had turned away; their wine jug refills itself, and the gods reward them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Generosity from scant means is miraculously replenished.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's cloud that will fill again, the generous couple's want is made good.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; next-best on generous poverty replenished, though Baucis and Philemon were never rich.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not easy for the liberal man to be rich, since he is not apt either at taking or at keeping, but at giving away, and does not value wealth for its own sake but as a means to giving. Hence comes the charge that is brought against fortune, that those who deserve riches most get it least.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that the generous often find themselves short of money precisely because they give.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the Kural's 'brief poverty' of the generous rich: it is the natural cost of their giving.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross, MIT Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; very close on the generous man's poverty, though without the image of renewal.
